# Abstract {.unnumbered}

{{< include _abstract.qmd >}}

**Keywords** Job satisfaction; Non-cognitive skills; Big Five personality; Working conditions; Occupational inequality; Cross-national comparison; PIAAC

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Two employees do the same job for the same pay and rate it differently. Job satisfaction is one of the main indicators through which statistical offices, international organizations, and employers assess the quality of working life [@cazes2015], whereas some scholars even treat it as one of the main components of subjective well-being [@sousa-poza2000; @vanpraag2003; @judgeklinger2008; @bowling2010]. These ratings also reflect workers' dispositions. The OECD's analysis of the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) finds that emotionally stable and extraverted adults are more satisfied with their jobs in nearly every participating country, and these associations "persist, albeit weaker" after accounting for wages, sector, and occupation [@oecd2025, p. 69]. If workers are more satisfied because they hold better jobs, satisfaction still measures the job. If personality affects how workers view and describe the same job, their ratings also reflect temperament. The distinction matters because job satisfaction is often read as evidence of job quality, while the same score may combine the conditions of a job with the worker's way of evaluating them.

Economists have estimated the wage returns to personality traits and their payoff in employment and occupation [@heckman2006; @almlund2011; @cobbclarkschurer2012]. Human capital theory treats personality traits as non-cognitive skills with a productive role [@humphries2017]. In the definition of @green2013, skills are productive, socially determined, and expandable through training and development. @cunha2007 model how such skills are produced over the life cycle, with skills acquired early raising the productivity of later investment (dynamic complementarity). Job satisfaction rarely appears in this body of work, although it predicts quitting and @freeman1978 treated it as an economic variable. Psychological and OECD studies of the personality gradient in satisfaction [@judge2002; @oecd2025] do not compare subjective and objective rewards in the same data. They also do not test why a trait is associated with higher satisfaction. The source of this established correlation between personality and job satisfaction is not yet clear.

The study uses PIAAC data from `r nC` high-income countries to examine the sources of the satisfaction premium and contributes to the literature in 3 ways. First, the subjective reward to non-cognitive skills is measured with the same instrument across national contexts. The *subjective reward* is defined as the association between a trait and job satisfaction at a given level of pay and background characteristics, and pay itself is the objective reward. Second, the study tests whether the premium reflects sorting into better jobs or a different view of the same job. Workers with productive non-cognitive skills may hold better jobs (*exposure*), respond differently to the same working conditions (*reactivity*), or report the same conditions differently (*appraisal*) [@bolger1995]. Earlier studies tested these routes only with diary data from single organizations and could not show whether workers with different traits hold different jobs. Finally, I estimate what the satisfaction gap between high and low occupational groups would be if the groups did not differ in personality profiles. This counterfactual gap splits the observed gap into the part accounted for by non-cognitive skills and the part accounted for by pay and working conditions.

Causal mediation analysis [@imai2010] is combined with a comparison of workers in the same job, defined by occupation and industry within each country. The mediation analysis gives the share of each premium that varies with pay and reported conditions. The within-job comparison is used to test whether the traits are associated with the jobs themselves or with how workers report them. The premiums are tested against omitted-variable bias [@oster2019], and the mediated parts are tested against unobserved confounding [@imai2010b]. To check whether the premiums reflect only a general tendency to report one's life favorably, I also hold life satisfaction fixed.

The results suggest that emotional stability has the largest premium, `r f2(tmean("EMOS"))` points on the 1–5 scale per standard deviation. The premiums for extraversion and agreeableness are `r f2(tmean("EXTR"))` and `r f2(tmean("AGRE"))`, respectively. Conscientiousness has a small premium. Open-mindedness has none. Pay carries `r pc(payshare("EMOS"))`% of the emotional-stability premium. Pay, job demands, job resources, and skill underuse together carry `r pc(medshare("EMOS"))`%, and the rest is direct. Workers with different traits hold similar jobs but report them differently. Within the same occupation and industry, less stable workers report more demands and also more resources than their colleagues. The premium is concentrated in low depression. Personality composition accounts for about a quarter of the satisfaction gap between high- and low-occupational groups.

The results matter for the use of job satisfaction as a quality-of-life indicator. Satisfaction gaps between groups of workers are often read as gaps in job quality, for example between women and men [@clark1997]. If part of satisfaction reflects how people appraise their jobs, these gaps also reflect who the workers are. Where personality is measured, researchers can estimate this component alongside the gap.

# Background and hypotheses {#sec-hyp}

Organizational psychology established that job attitudes have a dispositional component. Workers' satisfaction persists across job changes [@staw1985]. In the meta-analysis of @judge2002, the Big Five correlate with satisfaction at 0.29 for emotional stability, 0.26 for conscientiousness, 0.25 for extraversion, 0.17 for agreeableness, and 0.02 for openness. Because these estimates do not hold pay or occupation fixed, they cannot show whether satisfied workers earn more or hold better jobs. They also do not show how the association arises.

With the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills, the OECD extended the descriptive evidence across countries [@oecd2025]. In its estimates, a 1-standard-deviation increase in emotional stability is associated with a 6-percentage-point higher probability of high job satisfaction, and extraversion with 4 points, which is comparable to literacy. After accounting for wages and job characteristics, the association with literacy is no longer significant, whereas the associations with personality remain. The report interprets this as person–environment fit [@kristofbrown2005], or as emotion regulation, without testing either explanation. A recent study of young workers in 1 country also finds that the premium remains after controlling for wages and job characteristics [@avanesian2026]. These studies do not compare subjective and objective rewards. In the theory of compensating differentials [@rosen1986], a trait associated with satisfaction that the market does not pay for raises a further question. The question is whether workers with the trait hold better jobs or experience the same job differently.

@bolger1995 distinguish differential *exposure* to stressors from differential *reactivity* to them. A third route, differential *appraisal*, comes from @watson1984 on negative affectivity and refers to the tendency to report the same situation differently. In diary studies and single organizations, where these routes were tested, the same person reports both stressors and strain. Some studies therefore partial out negative affectivity as a nuisance, while others treat it as a cause [@spector2000]. Representative data with occupation codes allow each worker's report of a condition to be compared with the average report of workers in the same occupation and industry. Measurement choices of this kind have been linked to quitting [@pelly2023] and job-quality rankings [@stephens2025].

> **H1 (Subjective reward).** Holding pay fixed, emotional stability, extraversion, and agreeableness are associated with higher job satisfaction. The direction for conscientiousness and open-mindedness is unclear; their bivariate correlations are positive [@judge2002], but their adjusted associations vary across countries [@oecd2025].

The first route is *exposure*. The job demands–resources model describes job quality through 2 groups of conditions [@karasek1979; @bakker2007]. Demands such as time pressure, repetitive or physically strenuous work, and constant change drain workers. Resources such as autonomy and learning, or support and voice, motivate them. Emotionally stable workers may avoid high-strain jobs, and extraverts may find jobs with more contact and autonomy. If so, part of the premium moves with job conditions.

> **H2 (Exposure).** Part of the association between personality and satisfaction moves with reported working conditions. Emotional stability is associated with lower reported demands (H2a). Extraversion is associated with more resources, particularly autonomy and voice, as well as learning and social tasks (H2b).

The second route is *appraisal*. Negative affectivity is the core of low emotional stability. It colors reports of both stressors and satisfaction [@watson1984], and dispositional affect persists in job attitudes over long periods [@staw1985; @judge2001]. Under this account, traits predict how workers *report* their conditions relative to others in the same job, while the conditions themselves do not differ. The premium should then be concentrated in the affective component of the trait. Appraisal and sorting also make different predictions. A worker in a worse job than colleagues should report higher demands and fewer resources. A worker for whom the same work feels like more of everything should report more demands and also more resources.

> **H3 (Appraisal).** (a) Trait associations with reported conditions are concentrated in workers' deviations from their occupational-group means and are small in the group means. The part of the premium that moves with conditions moves with the deviations. Emotional stability predicts lower reports of demands and resources. (b) Within emotional stability, the premium is carried mainly by low depression. The difference between the depression and anxiety coefficients is distinguishable from zero.

The third route is *reactivity*. Trait activation theory holds that a trait matters where the situation calls for it [@tett2003]. Emotional stability should cushion the cost of demands, and social tasks should reward extraverts. Learning should reward the open-minded, and underuse should frustrate them. Autonomy should matter more to the conscientious, and support should matter more to the agreeable.

> **H4 (Reactivity).** Traits moderate the association between job conditions and satisfaction. Emotional stability weakens the cost of time pressure, repetitive work, and change (H4a). Extraversion strengthens the benefit of social tasks (H4b). Openness strengthens the benefit of learning and the cost of skill underuse (H4c). Conscientiousness strengthens the benefit of autonomy (H4d). Agreeableness strengthens the benefit of support (H4e).

Personality affects satisfaction comparisons between groups of workers only when the groups differ enough in personality composition, regardless of the route. Managers and professionals are on average more emotionally stable and extraverted than workers in operative and elementary occupations. Their satisfaction gap should therefore narrow when both groups have the same personality distribution. I chose this comparison before seeing the result. It is the widest contrast in occupational skill level that still leaves enough employees in each group in most countries.

> **H5 (Composition).** Within each country, the satisfaction gap between the high occupational group (ISCO 1–2) and the low one (ISCO 8–9) narrows when both groups are standardized to a common personality distribution. It narrows further when pay and reported conditions are adjusted for.

The 5 hypotheses run from reward size to its consequences. H1 concerns reward size. H2 to H4 concern its source, and H5 concerns its consequences for comparisons between groups of workers.

# Data {#sec-data}

I use the public-use files of the second cycle of PIAAC, fielded in 2022–2023 in representative samples of adults [@oecd2024]. Employed respondents rate their satisfaction with their current job on a 5-point scale. The main outcome is the 1–5 score (5 = extremely satisfied). The Big Five are measured with the 15-item BFI-2-XS and released as national z-scores, so a coefficient is the change in satisfaction per within-country standard deviation of the trait. In `r n_fac` countries, the 30-item BFI-2-S is also released, with 3 facets per trait [@soto2017]. The sample covers employees aged 25–65 in the `r nC` countries that release these variables. Only `r pc(min(ns_share))`% to `r pc(max(ns_share))`% of employees are neutral or dissatisfied (Appendix, Table A1). Samples and module coverage by country are in Table A2. Pay is the within-country decile of hourly earnings including bonuses, released for employees in `r n_pay` of the `r nC` countries. `r flagname` do not release an employee earnings measure. These 3 countries enter without the pay block and are marked with † in all figures. Respondents with a missing decile in a pay country are kept with a missing-pay indicator. Complete-case results are in Table A3.

The reported job conditions and their items are listed in Appendix Table A4. Because the appraisal hypothesis concerns the gap between a job and its report, I use the workers' own reports. Background controls are age band, sex, education, birthplace, parental education, and numeracy (mean of the 10 plausible values). Where stated, I also control for occupation, contract type, weekly hours, firm size, sector, and supervisory duties.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-desc
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics of the analysis sample by country (weighted)"
DS <- S$desc[order(cname[S$desc$country]), ]
tab <- data.frame(Country = ifelse(DS$country %in% flag, paste0(cname[DS$country], " †"), cname[DS$country]), N = big(DS$n),
  `Women (%)` = pc(DS$women), `Tertiary (%)` = pc(DS$tertiary), Numeracy = sprintf("%.0f", DS$numeracy),
  `Satisfaction (1–5)` = f2(DS$satisfaction), `Not satisfied (%)` = pc(DS$not_satisfied),
  `Time pressure (1–5)` = f2(DS$time_pressure), `Autonomy (1–5)` = f2(DS$autonomy), `Skill underuse (%)` = pc(DS$underuse),
  `Support and voice` = ifelse(DS$extended, "Yes", "No"), check.names = FALSE)
fin(kb(tab, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrrrrc"), size = 7, "Source: PIAAC Cycle 2 public-use files (OECD, 2024). Employees aged 25–65. Weighted with the final survey weight; N is the unweighted analysis sample. Numeracy: mean of the 10 plausible values (0–500 scale). Not satisfied: neither satisfied nor dissatisfied, dissatisfied, or extremely dissatisfied. Time pressure and autonomy are the raw item scales; skill underuse is the share reporting skills higher than the job requires. Support and voice: the extended module is fielded. † No earnings decile released.")
```

# Empirical strategy {#sec-strategy}

Every model is estimated separately in each country. For H1 and H2, causal mediation analysis is used [@imai2010], as shown in @fig-schematic. The treatment is a trait, and the effect is the change in satisfaction between workers 1 standard deviation apart in it, with the other 4 traits and the background controls $X_{ic}$ held fixed. The mediators are 4 blocks of variables: pay (the earnings decile), job demands (time pressure, repetitive tasks, physical work, and change), job resources (autonomy, learning, and social tasks, as well as support and voice in the `r n_ext` countries that measure them), and skill underuse. For worker $i$ in country $c$, the outcome equation regresses satisfaction $S_{ic}$ on the 5 traits $T_{kic}$, the controls, and all mediator variables: $$
S_{ic} = \alpha_c + \textstyle\sum_k c'_{kc} T_{kic} + \sum_{j} H_{jic} + X_{ic}'\gamma_c + \varepsilon_{ic}, \qquad H_{jic} = M_{jic}'b_{jc}.
$$ The index $H_{jic}$ is the contribution of block $j$, the variables $M_{jic}$ of the block weighted by their coefficients $b_{jc}$. A mediator equation regresses each index on the traits and controls, which gives the path $a_{kjc}$ from trait $k$ to block $j$. The average causal mediation effect (ACME) through block $j$ is the change in satisfaction that follows from the change in the block associated with 1 standard deviation of the trait; with linear equations, it equals $a_{kjc}$. The average direct effect (ADE) is $c'_{kc}$, the difference at the same values of all blocks. The ACMEs through the 4 blocks add up to the ACME through their sum, and the ACME through all blocks and the ADE add up to the *total effect*. The total effect includes any part of the premium that arises through pay. The premium *net of pay* is the total effect minus the ACME through pay, and H1 concerns it. Missing values of a condition are set to 0 with an indicator in its block, and a missing decile is set to the country mean with an indicator. In the `r nC - n_pay` countries without earnings deciles, the model has 3 blocks.

```{r}
#| label: fig-schematic
#| fig-cap: "The mediation model. A trait affects satisfaction directly (average direct effect, ADE) and through each mediator block (average causal mediation effect, ACME). For H3, each block of conditions is further split into the occupational-group mean and the worker's deviation from it."
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-width: 7
draw_schematic()
```

A causal reading of the ACMEs and the ADE requires that no unobserved factor affects both the condition and satisfaction once traits and controls are held fixed (sequential ignorability). The same person reports traits, conditions, and satisfaction at the same time. A common mood or a general disposition to describe one's situation favorably would violate this assumption. H3 tests for this disposition. Pay and the other controls may also partly be consequences of the trait [@bartram2021]. The decomposition is therefore interpreted as describing which conditions move with which traits and how much of the premium they account for. Adult personality is fairly stable [@cobbclarkschurer2012]. This stability limits reverse causality from the job to the trait reports. Sensitivity is checked in 4 ways. For the ACMEs, the error correlation between the mediator and outcome equations at which they would vanish is reported [@imai2010b]. For each premium, the coefficient that would remain if unobservables mattered as much as the observed controls is estimated [@oster2019]. The premium is also estimated conditional on life satisfaction. A last test looks for the tenure gradient that a gradual effect of the job on trait reports would produce.

For H3, each reported condition is split into the weighted leave-one-out mean among workers in the same group and the worker's deviation from that mean. Groups are country × finest released occupation × industry section, with a fallback to occupation alone where a group has fewer than 10 other members. The group mean is the average report in that kind of job. Without employer-level data, occupation-by-industry groups are the closest available reference point for the conditions attached to a type of work. Because workers in a group can still hold different jobs, the deviation contains real differences in conditions and the worker's reporting style. The group mean also reflects how people in the group tend to report. The split therefore cannot, by itself, separate the view of a job from unmeasured differences between jobs. It shows whether the trait associations are found in the group means or in the deviations. For each block of conditions, the mediation model is re-estimated with the group means and the deviations as separate blocks, so the ACME through a block splits into a part through the group means and a part through the deviations. The trait coefficients on the group means are tested for *equivalence* to zero with 2 one-sided tests and a margin of `r eq_margin_cell` SD. This margin is less than half the typical coefficient on the deviations, so a group-mean association inside it would be small next to the deviation association. I also test whether traits predict deviations in reported *resources* and demands. Tables A5 and A6 report the group definitions and re-estimates with stricter groups. For H3b, each trait is replaced with its 3 facets in the `r n_fac` countries that release them, and the depression–anxiety difference is tested directly.

For H4, the 8 hypothesized products and 3 placebo products with no proposed mechanism are added to each country's model with all conditions. Traits are centered and conditions standardized, so each product is the change in a condition's satisfaction slope per standard deviation of the trait. A product within ±`r eq_margin_int` points of zero, half a condition's own slope, is treated as equivalent to zero. Inside this margin, workers 1 standard deviation apart in the trait differ by less than half in how much the condition matters to them. Cross-sectional interactions compare different workers in different conditions, so they say little about how a single worker would react to a change.

For H5, 2 groups are compared in each country. The high group is managers and professionals (ISCO 1–2). The low group is plant and machine operators and workers in elementary occupations (ISCO 8–9). Where only the 4-level occupational skill variable is released, its top and bottom levels are compared. Satisfaction is regressed on the 5 traits separately in each group, and each group's mean is predicted at the pooled trait distribution. The difference between the 2 predictions is the gap that would remain if both groups had the same personality composition and kept their own trait coefficients. The further gaps add the pay decile and then the reported conditions, with common slopes.

All models are weighted with the final survey weight, and numeracy, literacy, and problem solving enter as the mean of their 10 plausible values. Countries are not pooled. The intervals of the mediation estimates are quasi-Bayesian approximations from 1,000 draws [@imai2010]. The other estimates are weighted least squares with conventional standard errors. Each figure shows the country estimates and their mean. The text reports significance from each country's own test. Counts after the Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment for multiple testing [@benjamini1995] are in Tables A7, A8 and A9.

The study follows the principles of literate statistical computing [@knuth1984]. The manuscript is written in Quarto [@allaire2024] with R [@rcore2025], and every number, table, and figure is computed from the public-use files by the code that accompanies it. The mediation estimates and their sensitivity analysis are outputs of the mediation package [version 4.5.1, @tingley2014].

# Results {#sec-results}

## The subjective reward to non-cognitive skills {#sec-h1}

@fig-h1 shows the total effect of each trait by country. At the same education, background, and numeracy, 1 standard deviation of emotional stability raises satisfaction by `r f2(tmean("EMOS"))` points on the 1–5 scale (range `r rng(TOT$estimate[TOT$var == "EMOS"], 2)`). The effect is positive in every country and significant at the 5% level in `r tsig("EMOS")` of `r nC`. Table A10 gives the country estimates. The total effect of extraversion is `r f2(tmean("EXTR"))` points (significant in `r tsig("EXTR")` countries) and that of agreeableness `r f2(tmean("AGRE"))` (`r tsig("AGRE")` countries). Conscientiousness has a small effect, `r f2(tmean("CONS"))` points (`r tsig("CONS")` countries). Open-mindedness has none (`r f2(tmean("OPEM"))`). This ordering matches the OECD's adjusted results on the same survey [@oecd2025] and differs from the bivariate correlations of @judge2002, where conscientiousness ranks second. Emotional stability is associated mainly with a lower probability of being neutral or dissatisfied, by `r rgK("not_satisfied", "EMOS")` percentage points (significant in `r kc("not_satisfied", "EMOS", -1)` countries). Extraversion is associated instead with a higher probability of being extremely satisfied (`r kc("very_satisfied", "EXTR", 1)` countries).

Little of the premium comes through pay. The ACME through the earnings decile is `r f3(amean("pay", "EMOS"))` points for emotional stability, `r pc(payshare("EMOS"))`% of the total effect in the `r n_pay` countries with deciles, and it is significant in `r npos("pay", "EMOS")` of them. Net of pay, the premium is `r f2(netpay("EMOS"))` points for emotional stability, `r f2(netpay("EXTR"))` for extraversion, and `r f2(netpay("AGRE"))` for agreeableness. In the weighted regressions with the pay decile as a control (Table A11), adding occupation changes the coefficients by `r pct1(occ_absorb("EMOS"))`% for emotional stability, `r pct1(occ_absorb("EXTR"))`% for extraversion, and `r pct1(occ_absorb("AGRE"))`% for agreeableness. With log hourly earnings instead of deciles, in the `r n_lw` countries that release them, the mean emotional-stability coefficient is `r f2(kmean("EMOS", KLW))` against `r f2(kmean("EMOS", KDW))`. The satisfaction difference between the top and the bottom earnings decile in the same model is `r f2(mean(PC$top_vs_bottom))` points on average across the `r nrow(PC)` countries with pay data. The emotional-stability coefficient per standard deviation is therefore about `r pc(mean(PC$emos) / mean(PC$top_vs_bottom))`% of the within-country pay gradient in satisfaction. The comparison uses 2 coefficients from the same model and sample and gives no monetary value. H1 is supported for emotional stability, extraversion, and agreeableness.

```{r}
#| label: fig-h1
#| fig-cap: "Total effect of each trait on job satisfaction, by country. Estimates from mediate(): change in the 1–5 satisfaction score per standard deviation of the trait, at the same education, background and numeracy; 95% intervals. Filled: p < 0.05; grey: p < 0.10; hollow: neither. Bottom row: mean across countries with 95% interval. † No earnings decile released."
#| fig-height: 7.2
#| fig-width: 12
u <- TOT[, c("country", "var", "estimate", "se", "lower", "upper", "p")]; u$panel <- tl[u$var]
fig_country_dots(u, tl, cname, flag, "Total effect per SD of the trait (points on the 1-5 scale), 95% interval")
```

## Exposure: little of the premium goes through the job {#sec-exposure}

@fig-indirect splits each country's total effect into the ACMEs through the 4 blocks and the ADE, and @tbl-med gives the means across countries. For emotional stability, the ADE is `r f2(dmean("EMOS"))` points, against a total effect of `r f2(tmean("EMOS"))`. The 4 blocks together carry `r f3(amean("all", "EMOS"))` points (`r pc(medshare("EMOS"))`%), significant in `r npos("all", "EMOS")` of `r nC` countries. Job demands carry the largest part, `r f3(amean("demands", "EMOS"))` points (positive and significant in `r npos("demands", "EMOS")` countries): emotionally stable workers report fewer demands, and demands lower satisfaction. Skill underuse adds `r f3(amean("underuse", "EMOS"))` (`r npos("underuse", "EMOS")` countries) and pay `r f3(amean("pay", "EMOS"))` (`r npos("pay", "EMOS")` of `r nmed("pay", "EMOS")`). Resources carry almost nothing (`r f3(amean("resources", "EMOS"))`). H2a receives weak support: the demands pathway is regular but small.

Extraversion has the only large pathway through the job. The ACME through resources is `r f3(amean("resources", "EXTR"))` points and positive and significant in `r npos("resources", "EXTR")` of `r nC` countries, so H2b is supported for resources. Extraverts also report more demands and more skill underuse, and these ACMEs are negative (`r f3(amean("demands", "EXTR"))` and `r f3(amean("underuse", "EXTR"))`; significant in `r nneg("demands", "EXTR")` and `r nneg("underuse", "EXTR")` countries). Pay adds `r f3(amean("pay", "EXTR"))`. The blocks together carry `r pc(medshare("EXTR"))`% of the extraversion effect. Open-mindedness shows the same pattern more sharply: a positive ACME through resources (`r npos("resources", "OPEM")` countries) is offset by negative ACMEs through demands and underuse, and its direct effect is close to zero. Agreeableness has almost no ACMEs; its effect is `r pc(dmean("AGRE") / tmean("AGRE"))`% direct.

@fig-sens shows how the ACMEs of emotional stability respond to unobserved confounding of the mediators. The error correlation $\rho^*$ at which the ACME would be zero is `r f2(rho_k(1))` for pay alone on average and rises to `r f2(rho_k(4))` when all 4 blocks are included. A factor that correlates only weakly with both the mediators and satisfaction could therefore account for the mediated part. A reporting disposition is one such factor.

```{r}
#| label: fig-indirect
#| fig-cap: "Causal mediation estimates by country: indirect effects of each trait through pay, job demands, job resources and skill underuse, and the direct effect. Bars to the right of zero raise satisfaction, bars to the left lower it; the parts add up to the total effect (circle, with 95% interval). Bottom row: means across countries. † No earnings decile released."
#| fig-height: 7.6
#| fig-width: 12
tv <- c("EMOS", "EXTR", "AGRE")
parts <- rbind(do.call(rbind, lapply(names(blk), function(m) { u <- AC[AC$mediator == m & AC$var %in% tv, ]
    data.frame(country = u$country, panel = tl[u$var], part = blk[[m]], value = u$estimate) })),
  { u <- ADE[ADE$var %in% tv, ]; data.frame(country = u$country, panel = tl[u$var], part = "Direct effect", value = u$estimate) })
tt <- TOT[TOT$var %in% tv, c("country", "var", "estimate", "se", "lower", "upper", "p")]; tt$panel <- tl[tt$var]
fig_blocks_by_country(parts, tt, unname(tl[tv]), cname, flag, "Effect per SD of the trait (points on the 1-5 scale); circle = total effect, 95% interval")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-med
#| tbl-cap: "Causal mediation estimates: average causal mediation effect (ACME) of each trait through pay, job demands, job resources and skill underuse, average direct effect (ADE), and total effect (mean of countries)"
fin(kb(med_table(names(blk), paste("ACME:", tolower(blk))), row.names = FALSE, align = "lccccc"), size = 8,
  sprintf("Source: PIAAC Cycle 2 public-use files (OECD, 2024). *** p < 0.01, ** p < 0.05, * p < 0.10. Output of mediate() (Tingley et al., 2014) from weighted linear mediator and outcome equations (Imai, Keele & Yamamoto, 2010), estimated in each of the %d countries with %s quasi-Bayesian draws; entries are means of the country estimates (points on the 1–5 scale per SD of the trait) with the 95%% interval of the mean below. Each block enters as the index of its variables weighted by their coefficients in the outcome equation with all blocks; the block ACMEs add up to the indirect effect through all blocks. Pay: %d countries. Proportion mediated: sum of the block ACMEs over the total effect.", nC, big(med_info$sims), n_pay))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sens
#| fig-cap: "Sensitivity of the mediation estimates to unobserved confounding of the mediators, from medsens() (emotional stability). Panel a: ρ*, the correlation between the errors of the mediator and outcome equations at which the ACME through the listed blocks is zero, by country; dashed line: mean of countries. Panel b: mean ACME across countries at each assumed error correlation, as a percentage of the mean ACME at ρ = 0."
#| fig-height: 7.5
#| fig-width: 11
bl <- c("Pay", "+ demands", "+ resources", "+ skill underuse")
fig_sensitivity(RHO, GRID, cname, bl)
```

## Appraisal: the association is in the deviations {#sec-appraisal}

@tbl-split splits the ACMEs through demands and resources into the part through the occupational group's mean and the part through the worker's deviation from it. Nearly all of each ACME goes through the deviation. For emotional stability, the ACME through the deviations in demands is `r f3(amean("demands_dev", "EMOS"))` points (positive and significant in `r npos("demands_dev", "EMOS")` of `r nmed("demands_dev", "EMOS")` countries), and that through the group means `r f3(amean("demands_mean", "EMOS"))` (`r npos("demands_mean", "EMOS") + nneg("demands_mean", "EMOS")` countries). Among the single conditions (Table A12), the deviation in time pressure carries most of it (`r npos("time_pressure_dev", "EMOS")` countries). For extraversion, the ACME through the deviations in resources is `r f3(amean("resources_dev", "EXTR"))` (`r npos("resources_dev", "EXTR")` countries), mainly through voice, autonomy and learning, and that through the group means `r f3(amean("resources_mean", "EXTR"))` (`r npos("resources_mean", "EXTR")` countries). Extraverts thus also work in groups that report somewhat more resources, but a smaller part of their pathway goes through the group mean.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-split
#| tbl-cap: "Group mean or individual deviation? ACME of each trait through the occupational-group mean and through the worker's deviation from it, by block of reported conditions (mean of countries)"
sl <- c(split_pay = "ACME: pay", demands_mean = "ACME: job demands, group mean", demands_dev = "ACME: job demands, deviation",
  resources_mean = "ACME: job resources, group mean", resources_dev = "ACME: job resources, deviation", split_underuse = "ACME: skill underuse")
tb <- med_table(names(sl), unname(sl)); tb <- tb[!tb[[1]] %in% c("ADE: direct effect", "Total effect"), ]
fin(kb(tb, row.names = FALSE, align = "lccccc"), size = 8, sprintf("Source: PIAAC Cycle 2 public-use files (OECD, 2024). *** p < 0.01, ** p < 0.05, * p < 0.10. Output of mediate() as in Table 2, %d countries (Austria and Germany release no occupation or industry codes). Each reported condition is split into the weighted leave-one-out mean of the worker's occupation-by-industry group and the worker's deviation from it; each part enters as an index weighted by its coefficients in the outcome equation with all parts. Proportion mediated: over the total effect of Table 2. Country estimates for each condition in Table A12.", n_a1))
```

@fig-perceived shows the trait coefficients on both parts of each condition. Emotionally stable workers report less time pressure than others in the same occupation and industry in `r pneg("time_pressure")` of `r n_a1` countries (sign test p `r fmtp(signp(pneg("time_pressure"), n_a1))`; significant in `r sum(perc("time_pressure")$p < .05 & perc("time_pressure")$estimate < 0)`). They also report less change, physical strain, learning, and social contact, each in at least `r min(sapply(c('change', 'physical', 'learning', 'social'), pneg))` of `r n_a1` countries. Less stable workers thus report higher demands and also more resources. Worse jobs, or a uniformly negative way of reporting, would raise demands and lower resources, so the pattern points to experiencing the same work as more intense. The coefficients on the group means are close to zero. For time pressure, the coefficient of emotional stability on the group mean is within ±`r eq_margin_cell` SD, with its 90% interval, in `r equiv(actsel("time_pressure"), eq_margin_cell)` of `r n_a1` countries (nominally significant in `r sum(actsel("time_pressure")$p < .05)`). Its minimum detectable effect is `r f3(2.8 * median(actsel("time_pressure")$se))` SD, against a typical deviation coefficient of `r f3(abs(median(perc("time_pressure")$estimate)))` SD. Extraverts report more voice, autonomy, learning, and social tasks than others in their group. The results are unchanged with minimum group sizes of 20 and 30 and with 1-digit occupations in every country (Table A6). H3a is supported. The design cannot exclude within-group differences in actual conditions that the occupation codes miss and that go in the same direction.

```{r}
#| label: fig-perceived
#| fig-cap: "Coefficients of emotional stability and extraversion on the worker's deviation from the occupational-group mean and on the group mean (SD per SD): cross-country mean with 95% interval; grey dots: countries. Right: countries significant at the 5% level (+/−). Austria and Germany excluded. Full results in Appendix, Table A13."
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-width: 11
row_m <- function(x, panel, item) { r <- summ(x)[1, ]
  data.frame(panel = panel, item = item, estimate = r$estimate, lower = r$lower, upper = r$upper,
    lab = count_label(sum(x$p < .05 & x$estimate > 0), sum(x$p < .05 & x$estimate < 0), nrow(x)), highlight = FALSE) }
pp <- c("Emotional stability:\ndeviation", "Emotional stability:\ngroup mean", "Extraversion:\ndeviation", "Extraversion:\ngroup mean")
P <- do.call(rbind, lapply(conds, function(k) rbind(row_m(perc(k), pp[1], cl[[k]]), row_m(actsel(k), pp[2], cl[[k]]),
  row_m(perc(k, "EXTR"), pp[3], cl[[k]]), row_m(actsel(k, "EXTR"), pp[4], cl[[k]]))))
P$panel <- factor(P$panel, levels = pp); P$item <- factor(P$item, levels = rev(unname(cl[conds])))
bgP <- do.call(rbind, lapply(conds, function(k) rbind(data.frame(panel = pp[1], item = cl[[k]], estimate = perc(k)$estimate), data.frame(panel = pp[2], item = cl[[k]], estimate = actsel(k)$estimate),
  data.frame(panel = pp[3], item = cl[[k]], estimate = perc(k, "EXTR")$estimate), data.frame(panel = pp[4], item = cl[[k]], estimate = actsel(k, "EXTR")$estimate))))
bgP$panel <- factor(bgP$panel, levels = pp); bgP$item <- factor(bgP$item, levels = levels(P$item))
fig_means(P, "Mean coefficient across countries (SD of the condition per SD of the trait), 95% interval", band_last = FALSE, bg = bgP, x_pad = 0.55) + facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1)
```

@fig-facets shows that low depression, the facet that measures sadness and low mood, accounts for the emotional-stability premium. Its coefficient is positive and significant in `r if (fsig("EMOS_DEPR") == n_fac) paste("all", n_fac) else paste(fsig("EMOS_DEPR"), "of the", n_fac)` countries with facet scores (mean `r f3(fmean("EMOS_DEPR"))` points per SD). A stress-buffering account would single out low anxiety. Its coefficient is significant in `r fsig("EMOS_ANXI")` `r if (fsig("EMOS_ANXI") == 1) "country" else "countries"`. Low volatility is significant in `r fsig("EMOS_VOLA")`. The depression–anxiety difference is `r f3(fdiff("EMOS_DEPR-EMOS_ANXI")[["mean"]])` points on average (95% interval `r f3(fdiff("EMOS_DEPR-EMOS_ANXI")[["lo"]])` to `r f3(fdiff("EMOS_DEPR-EMOS_ANXI")[["hi"]])`) and significant in `r fdiff("EMOS_DEPR-EMOS_ANXI")[["pos"]]` of `r n_fac` countries. Within extraversion, energy, the facet closest to positive affect, is the only facet whose mean across countries is distinguishable from zero. The facets associated with satisfaction are those closest to positive and negative affect, as H3b predicts. The low-depression facet measures a general tendency toward low mood and is not a clinical measure. Because it is close to evaluative well-being, the result suggests that the personality component of job satisfaction also relates to how people evaluate other life domains.

```{r}
#| label: fig-facets
#| fig-cap: "Coefficients of the 15 BFI-2 facets on the 1–5 satisfaction score, entered together with pay decile and controls, in the 12 countries with facet scores: cross-country mean with 95% interval; grey dots: countries. Right: countries significant at the 5% level (+/−). Country estimates in Appendix, Fig. A1."
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-width: 9
fls <- sub("^[A-Z]+: ", "", fl); fls <- sub("^\\(low\\)", "(Low)", fls); substr(fls, 1, 1) <- toupper(substr(fls, 1, 1))
FAo <- FA[FA$outcome == o & FA$var %in% names(fl), ]
Fq <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fl), function(f) { x <- FAo[FAo$var == f, ]; r <- summ(x)[1, ]
  data.frame(panel = tl[[sub("_.*", "", f)]], item = fls[[f]], estimate = r$estimate, lower = r$lower, upper = r$upper,
    lab = count_label(sum(x$p < .05 & x$estimate > 0), sum(x$p < .05 & x$estimate < 0), nrow(x)), highlight = FALSE) }))
Fq$panel <- factor(Fq$panel, levels = tl); Fq$item <- factor(Fq$item, levels = rev(unname(fls)))
bg <- data.frame(panel = factor(tl[sub("_.*", "", FAo$var)], levels = tl), item = factor(fls[FAo$var], levels = levels(Fq$item)), estimate = FAo$estimate)
fig_means(Fq, "Satisfaction points per SD of the facet, 95% interval", band_last = FALSE, bg = bg, x_pad = 0.3, label_at = max(bg$estimate) + 0.01) +
  facet_grid(panel ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside", strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), strip.background = element_blank())
```

## Reactivity: small interactions between traits and reported conditions {#sec-reactivity}

@fig-reactivity shows the 8 pre-specified products and the 3 placebos. Of the `r r_tested_n` country estimates of the pre-specified products, `r r_nom_tested` are significant at the 5% level, about twice the `r round(0.05 * r_tested_n)` expected if all products were zero, and most have the predicted sign. The placebo products are significant in `r r_nom_placebo` of `r r_placebo_n` estimates. Emotional stability × time pressure and openness × learning have the predicted sign in `r rsum("R1")[["sameside"]]` of `r nC` countries (sign test p `r fmtp(signp(rsum("R1")[["sameside"]], nC))` for each), with mean products of `r f3(rsum("R1")[["mean"]])` and `r f3(rsum("R5")[["mean"]])` points per SD × SD. In a single country, I can detect only products of about `r f3(mde_med)` points, as large as a condition's own satisfaction slope. Of the country estimates, `r sum(sapply(tested, function(p) rsum(p)[["equiv"]]))` of `r r_tested_n` are equivalent to zero. The cross-country means are more precise. The largest is `r f3(max(abs(sapply(tested, function(p) rsum(p)[["mean"]]))))` points, against condition slopes of 0.05 to 0.10 points. H4 is not supported in the sense of large moderation. Small moderation in the predicted direction for emotional stability and openness remains compatible with the data. Table A9 gives the full results.

```{r}
#| label: fig-reactivity
#| fig-cap: "All trait × condition products: change in a condition's satisfaction slope per SD of the trait (points per SD × SD), mean of country estimates; each product estimated in a model with all conditions. Below the mean: countries with p < 0.05 / countries estimated. Outlined: the 8 pre-specified products (H4); the 3 placebo products are among the others."
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-width: 10
PR <- CH[CH$model == "PROD" & CH$kind == "prod", ]; PR$trait <- sub(":.*", "", PR$var); PR$cond <- sub(".*:", "", PR$var)
cl_h <- c(cl[c("time_pressure", "repetitive", "physical", "change", "autonomy", "learning", "social", "support", "voice")], underuse = "Skill underuse")
H <- do.call(rbind, lapply(traits, function(v) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cl_h), function(k) { u <- PR[PR$trait == v & PR$cond == k, ]
  data.frame(trait = tl[[v]], condition = cl_h[[k]], estimate = mean(u$estimate), n_sig = sum(u$p < .05), n = nrow(u)) }))))
H$trait <- factor(H$trait, levels = rev(tl)); H$condition <- factor(H$condition, levels = unname(cl_h))
ol <- pair_def[pair_def$sign != 0, ]; ol <- data.frame(trait = factor(tl[ol$trait], levels = rev(tl)), condition = factor(cl_h[ol$condition], levels = unname(cl_h)))
fig_heatmap(H, ol)
```

## Composition: what the personality mix of worker groups changes {#sec-indicator}

@fig-gap shows the satisfaction gap between the high and low occupational groups in the `r n_ind` countries with occupation codes and at least 100 employees in each group. The raw gap is `r f2(mean(gap("raw")$estimate))` points on average (range `r rng(gap("raw")$estimate, 2)`) and significantly positive in `r sum(gap("raw")$p < .05 & gap("raw")$estimate > 0)` countries. When I standardize both groups to the pooled personality distribution, the gap falls by `r f2(median(abs(gap_change("raw", "standardised"))))` points at the median across countries (largest change `r f2(max(abs(gap_change("raw", "standardised"))))`), to `r f2(mean(gap("standardised")$estimate))` on average. Personality composition therefore accounts for `r pc(median(abs(gap_change("raw", "standardised")) / abs(gap("raw")$estimate)))`% of the gap at the median. When I add the pay decile, the gap becomes `r f2(mean(gap("traits_pay")$estimate))`. When I also add reported conditions, it becomes `r f2(mean(gap("traits_pay_conditions")$estimate))`. At the same pay and conditions, the lower group is as satisfied as the higher one or slightly more. Pay and conditions account for most of the gap. Personality accounts for a smaller part, as H5 predicts.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gap
#| fig-cap: "Satisfaction gap (1–5 scale) between managers and professionals (ISCO 1–2) and operative and elementary occupations (ISCO 8–9): raw, with both groups standardized to the pooled personality distribution, then adding the pay decile and the core reported conditions. Croatia and New Zealand use occupational skill levels; Ireland is excluded. Markers and † as in Fig. 2."
#| fig-height: 6.8
#| fig-width: 12
gl <- c(raw = "Raw gap", standardised = "Personality-\nstandardized", traits_pay = "+ pay decile", traits_pay_conditions = "+ pay and\nconditions")
u <- IND[IND$var %in% names(gl), c("country", "var", "estimate", "se", "lower", "upper", "p")]; u$panel <- gl[u$var]
fig_country_dots(u, unname(gl), cname, flag, "Satisfaction gap between the high and the low occupational group (points on the 1-5 scale), 95% interval") + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 9.5, lineheight = 0.9))
```

## Sensitivity and robustness {#sec-robust}

Following @oster2019, I assume that unobservables matter as much as the observed controls (δ = 1, Rmax = 1.3 × R²). Under this assumption, the emotional-stability coefficient remains positive in `r sum(OS$trait == "EMOS" & OS$beta_star > 0)` of `r nC` countries. Its mean is `r f3(mean(OS$beta_star[OS$trait == "EMOS"]))` against an observed `r f3(mean(OS$b_full[OS$trait == "EMOS"]))` (Table A14). @masten2022 show that a coefficient can change sign with far less confounding than it takes to reach zero, so this result describes sensitivity to a single assumption. When I condition on life satisfaction, I remove a reporting disposition and any effect of a good job on a good life, so the result is not a bound. With this control, the emotional-stability premium is significant in `r sum(LSL$var == "EMOS" & LSL$p < .05 & LSL$estimate > 0)` of `r nC` countries. In the `r n_ten` countries that release tenure, `r if (sum(TEN$p < .05) == 0) "no trait × long-tenure product is significant" else paste0("trait × long-tenure products are significant in ", sum(TEN$p < .05), " of ", nrow(TEN), " cases")`. An immediate or non-monotonic effect of the job on trait reports would not show in this test. Table A15 summarizes what each check can establish.

The baseline premiums are unchanged in logit models, with literacy instead of numeracy, with the 6-item trait scales, with a tenure control, and with the self-employed included (Table A3).

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The subjective reward to non-cognitive skills is large compared with the objective one. For 1 standard deviation of emotional stability, the satisfaction premium is about `r pc(mean(PC$emos) / mean(PC$top_vs_bottom))`% of the within-country pay gradient in satisfaction, and only `r pc(payshare("EMOS"))`% of the premium goes through pay. Wage returns estimated elsewhere, a few % of wages per standard deviation [@heckman2006; @almlund2011], are measured in different units and samples and cannot be compared directly. In the framework of @rosen1986, workers with these traits bring to any job a satisfaction premium equivalent to a third of the pay gradient in satisfaction. In these data, little of this premium is reflected in pay. The results below suggest that it does not come from the jobs themselves either. On this interpretation, the subjective rewards to these skills exceed the objective ones. Personality is associated at least as strongly with intrinsic career success as with the extrinsic success measured by wages and employment.

Little of the satisfaction premium is associated with better jobs (H2). Extraversion is a partial exception. Extraverts report more autonomy, learning, and voice, consistent with sorting into occupations with more influence and contact [@cobbclarkschurer2012; @oecd2025]. They also report more time pressure and skill underuse, and these pathways offset part of the gain from resources. Traits are linked to the jobs workers hold, but in these estimates the 4 blocks carry `r pc(medshare("EMOS"))`% of the emotional-stability premium and `r pc(medshare("EXTR"))`% of the extraversion premium.

Most of the reward is associated with how workers report their jobs (H3). The group means are equivalent across traits within a margin of a third of the deviation coefficient, and the part of the premium that moves with conditions moves with the deviations. The premium is concentrated in low depression, while low anxiety has little association with it. Negative affectivity has been treated either as a nuisance that inflates stressor–strain correlations or as a substantive trait that shapes exposure and reaction [@watson1984; @spector2000]. The results for the satisfaction premium suggest a third role, in which negative affectivity shapes how workers perceive their jobs, mainly through its depressive side. This study extends the diary and single-organization studies in that debate with representative data. Each worker's report is compared with an external reference point, the average report in that worker's occupation and industry.

Traits hardly change the association between conditions and satisfaction (H4). Contrary to trait activation theory [@tett2003] and person–environment fit [@kristofbrown2005], at the cross-country mean, the pre-specified products are a tenth of a condition's own slope. Given the power of the tests, I can exclude large moderation, but I cannot rule out small moderation in the predicted direction. In models of job amenities, workers may value conditions differently. Along personality lines, these valuation differences are small, at least for the conditions measured in this survey. The main effects of autonomy, learning, voice, time pressure, and skill underuse are large and similar for workers with different traits.

The reward also matters for comparisons between groups of workers (H5). About a quarter of the satisfaction gap between high and low occupational groups reflects their composition in these traits. At the same pay and conditions, the lower group is as satisfied as the higher one or more. Comparisons of satisfaction across groups that differ in personality composition, by occupation, sex, age or health, include this component. Satisfaction gaps between groups of workers therefore combine unequal job quality with differences in the traits that shape how workers evaluate and report their work.

All variables are self-reported at a single point in time. A causal reading of the decomposition requires sequential ignorability. The appraisal results cast doubt on that assumption. Panel data with repeated measures of personality and conditions would establish temporal order [@maxwell2007]. Linked employer–employee data, with the workplace as the group, would distinguish a worker who sees the same job differently from one who holds a different job within the same codes. Regarding scale equivalence across languages, I rely on the instrument's validation [@soto2017].

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

Across `r nC` countries, emotionally stable, extraverted, and agreeable employees are more satisfied with their jobs than other workers with the same pay and occupation. Pay and reported working conditions carry little of this premium. It is associated mainly with how workers report their jobs and, within emotional stability, with low depression. Personality composition accounts for about a quarter of the satisfaction gap between broad occupational groups. `r pc(payshare("EMOS"))`% of the emotional-stability premium goes through pay, so workers with these traits are more satisfied mainly at the same level of pay. Non-cognitive skills are therefore associated with intrinsic as well as extrinsic career success.
